questions.question: Q: What are the advantages of a geostationary orbit?

points.text: The satellite remains above the same point on Earth, so ground antennas don't need to track it. Ideal for communications and weather monitoring of a fixed region.

questions.question: Q: Why are polar orbits useful for Earth observation?

points.text: The satellite passes over different parts of Earth on each orbit as the planet rotates beneath it, eventually covering the entire surface — ideal for mapping and environmental monitoring.

questions.question: Q: Name three types of space probe and their functions.

points.text: Orbiter: orbits a body for long-term remote study (e.g. Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter). Lander: touches down to study the surface in situ (e.g. Philae). Rover: a mobile lander that can explore multiple locations (e.g. Curiosity).

questions.question: Q: What is the Kessler syndrome?

points.text: A cascading effect where collisions between space debris create more debris, potentially making certain orbits too dangerous to use.

questions.question: Q: Calculate the orbital period of a satellite at 35,786 km altitude using Kepler's 3rd law.

points.text: A satellite at this altitude (geostationary orbit) has an orbital period of exactly 24 hours, matching Earth's rotation — this is the definition of geostationary orbit.
